title: Adam and Eve (24 December)
hook: some old calendars honor our first parents on Christmas Eve

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kanty, the professor with bare feet under his gown. Your line was the professor's coat. Did a coat make it into a bag by the door? Day one thousand fifty-six.

On the day before Christmas, some old calendars of saints didn't name a martyr or a bishop. They named two people from the very first pages of the Bible: Adam and Eve. Tradition says that in parts of medieval Europe, people acted out the story of the garden around this day, with a tree hung with fruit standing in the middle of the stage. Some historians connect that tree, at least in part, with the Christmas tree. So why would anyone put the garden right next to the manger?
screen: `CHRISTMAS EVE IN OLD CALENDARS.` → `A TREE HUNG WITH FRUIT.` → `THE GARDEN NEXT TO THE MANGER.`

segments.voice: Start with how Genesis tells it. In the Douay-Rheims: "And the Lord God formed man of the slime of the earth: and breathed into his face the breath of life, and man became a living soul." Mud and breath. That's the human being in this story: made of the ground, alive with God's own breath. Then the woman, made from Adam's side, and a garden with one tree whose fruit they are told not to eat. The rest is the famous part. Notice that the text never says apple; it says the fruit of the tree. The apple came later, in art and plays. They eat, they hide, they are sent out of the garden. And before they leave, Adam names his wife. "And Adam called the name of his wife Eve, because she was the mother of all the living." Even on the edge of leaving paradise, the story puts a name of life on her. That's why the day before Christmas fits. Catholic tradition reads the Bible as one story, and Christmas as a turning point in it. Paul puts the two ends side by side: "And as in Adam all die, so also in Christ all shall be made alive." He even calls Christ the last Adam. Early Christian writers added a second pair, calling Mary the new Eve, the woman whose yes undoes the first no. So on Christmas Eve, the old calendars remembered the first parents, waiting, as it were, at the door of the stable. And there's one more thing in Eve's name. If she is the mother of all the living, then every person you will meet today is, in this story, a cousin.
screen: `MUD AND BREATH: A LIVING SOUL.` · `THE FRUIT, NOT AN APPLE.` · `EVE: MOTHER OF ALL THE LIVING.` · `IN ADAM ALL DIE; IN CHRIST, ALIVE.` · then, large: `THE MOTHER OF ALL THE LIVING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold the whole human family. Settle, and notice your breath, the breath of life in the story. Begin with one face, someone close to you. Then widen: the people on your street. Your town. The people you argue with. Strangers on the other side of the world, waking up as you go to sleep. Let the circle keep growing until it holds everyone. If you pray, you can say the first two words of the Lord's Prayer, Our Father, and notice the word our. If you don't, simply let the word family stretch as far as it will go. The bell holds the time.
Eve. In Genesis, with Adam, the first parents, made of earth and breath, remembered in some old calendars on Christmas Eve, the night the story turns.

Your line: the first parents. Today, when someone gets on your nerves, remember that in this story they are family, and treat them like a cousin you'll see again at the holidays. Day one thousand fifty-six.

howItsDone: Adam and Eve are not on today's General Roman Calendar, but some older Western calendars and devotions remembered them on 24 December, and Catholics hear the garden story at Mass on the feast of the Immaculate Conception, where it is set beside Mary.

notes: Confirm Challoner wording of Genesis 2:7, Genesis 3:20 and 1 Corinthians 15:22.

The 24 December commemoration of Adam and Eve in some medieval Western calendars and martyrologies, and the paradise plays with a fruit-hung tree, are attributed to tradition; the link to the Christmas tree is attributed to 'some historians'. Confirm both.
'The apple came later, in art and plays' is a claim about tradition rather than the text; confirm phrasing.
Genesis 3:20 comes after the sentence in 3:16–19 and before the expulsion in 3:23; 'on the way out' is a loose summary. Confirm.
'Catholic tradition reads the Bible as one long story, with Christmas as a turning point. is a general description; Keeper may soften.
Mary as the new Eve attributed to 'early Christian writers' (Justin Martyr, Irenaeus); confirm the source citation.

Audit: teach said the tree was one 'they are told not to touch'; God's command in Genesis 2:17 is not to eat of it (touching appears only in the woman's words in 3:3). Corrected to 'whose fruit they are told not to eat'.

Editor pass: 'on the way out' (teach and fork) changed to 'before they leave', since Genesis 3:20 comes before the expulsion in 3:23; howItsDone no longer cites the Easter Vigil (its Genesis reading is the creation account, not the garden story) and instead names the Immaculate Conception Mass, whose first reading is Genesis 3:9–15, 20; confirm.
